title: Der, die, das — noun gender patterns
theoryMd:
German gives every noun one of three genders: **masculine** (*der*), **feminine** (*die*) or **neuter** (*das*). The gender is a property of the word, not of the thing it describes — *das Mädchen* (the girl) is neuter, *der Löffel* (the spoon) is masculine. This is why you should always learn a noun **with its article**: not *Tisch* but *der Tisch*.

The good news is that German gender is far more predictable than most courses admit. Roughly 80% of nouns are covered by rules about how the word **ends**. Learn the endings and you can guess correctly most of the time.

## Endings that are almost always feminine

These are the most reliable rules in the whole system. Treat them as certainties.

| Ending | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **-ung** | die Wohnung | flat |
| **-heit** | die Freiheit | freedom |
| **-keit** | die Möglichkeit | possibility |
| **-schaft** | die Freundschaft | friendship |
| **-tion** | die Nation | nation |
| **-tät** | die Universität | university |
| **-ie** | die Energie | energy |
| **-ik** | die Musik | music |

Also feminine: most nouns ending in **-e** (*die Lampe*, *die Straße*, *die Sprache*) — around 90% of them. The main exceptions are the weak masculine nouns for people and animals (*der Junge*, *der Kollege*, *der Löwe*) and a handful of neuters (*das Auge*, *das Ende*, *das Interesse*).

## Endings that are almost always neuter

| Ending | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **-chen** | das Mädchen | girl |
| **-lein** | das Fräulein | young lady |
| **-ment** | das Dokument | document |
| **-um** | das Zentrum | centre |
| **-tum** | das Eigentum | property |

*-chen* and *-lein* are diminutive endings, and they **override** the gender of the original word. *Die Frau* becomes *das Frauchen*; *der Hund* becomes *das Hündchen*. This is exactly why *das Mädchen* is neuter — it is a diminutive of the old word *die Magd*.

One more very productive rule: **any infinitive used as a noun is neuter**. *Essen* (to eat) → *das Essen* (the food, the meal). *Leben* → *das Leben*. You can do this with any verb, and the result is always *das*.

## Endings that are almost always masculine

| Ending | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **-er** (person/agent) | der Lehrer | teacher |
| **-ling** | der Lehrling | apprentice |
| **-ismus** | der Kapitalismus | capitalism |
| **-or** | der Motor | engine |
| **-ant** | der Elefant | elephant |

Also masculine, by meaning rather than ending:

- days, months and seasons — *der Montag*, *der Juli*, *der Sommer*
- weather phenomena — *der Regen*, *der Schnee*, *der Wind* (but *das Gewitter*)
- points of the compass — *der Norden*, *der Süden*
- makes of car — *der BMW*, *der Golf*
- alcoholic drinks — *der Wein*, *der Schnaps* (but *das Bier*)

> Careful with **-er**: it is masculine when it means a person or a tool doing something (*der Fahrer*, *der Computer*), but plenty of common non-agent nouns in *-er* are neuter or feminine — *das Fenster*, *das Wasser*, *die Butter*, *die Mutter*.

## Compound nouns: the last word decides

This rule is absolute and enormously useful. In a compound, the **final element** determines the gender of the whole thing:

- *die Tür* + *der Griff* → **der** Türgriff (door handle)
- *der Hand* + *die Tasche* → **die** Handtasche (handbag)
- *das Haus* + *die Aufgabe* → **die** Hausaufgabe (homework)
- *die Arbeit* + *das Zimmer* → **das** Arbeitszimmer (study)

So you never need to learn a compound separately. If you know *die Zeitung*, you know *die Tageszeitung*, *die Wochenzeitung*, *die Lokalzeitung*.

## When you genuinely cannot tell

Some very common short nouns simply have to be memorised: *der Tisch*, *die Uhr*, *das Buch*, *der Stuhl*, *das Bett*, *die Tür*. There is no pattern — but there are only a few hundred of them, and they are the words you meet constantly, so they come quickly.

A practical trick when you meet a new noun in the wild: look at the article or adjective ending in the sentence. *Ich habe **einen** neuen Tisch gekauft* tells you *Tisch* is masculine, because *einen* is the masculine accusative form. The sentence you saved the word from usually contains the answer.

> One warning about the plural: **all** plural nouns take *die*, whatever their singular gender. *der Tisch → die Tische*, *das Buch → die Bücher*. Seeing *die* therefore does not prove a noun is feminine — it might be a plural.

payload.explanation: Nouns ending in -ung are feminine: die Wohnung.
The diminutive ending -chen always makes a noun neuter, regardless of the original word's gender.
-er denoting a person who does something is masculine: der Lehrer.
Nouns in -um are neuter: das Zentrum, das Museum, das Datum.
In a compound the LAST element decides. Tasche is feminine, so die Handtasche.
The last element Griff is masculine, so the whole compound is masculine — even though Tür is feminine.

payload.prompt: You turn the verb 'essen' into a noun. Which article does it take?
payload.explanation: Any infinitive used as a noun is neuter: das Essen, das Leben, das Lesen.

payload.prompt: Which of these is NOT feminine?
payload.explanation: Most nouns in -e are feminine, but weak masculine nouns for people and animals are the exception: der Junge, der Kollege, der Löwe.
Days, months and seasons are masculine: der Montag, der Juli, der Sommer.

payload.prompt: You see 'die Tische' in a text. What does that tell you about the gender of 'Tisch'?
payload.explanation: All plurals take die, whatever the singular gender. Tisch is in fact masculine: der Tisch, die Tische.
